I don't think it's comic book movies so much as movie adaptations of proven popular source material. E.g., regular books/novels (Jurassic Park, Lord of the Rings, Hunger Games, Harry Potter, etc.), TV shows (Mission Impossible, Charlie's Angels, The A Team, etc.), toys (Transformers, Trolls, The Lego Movie, etc.)

Producers are loathe to risk investing in something they can't quantify and consumers actually prefer an established universe where they already know the rules and the characters and can get straight into the meat of the story--sometimes especially if the familiar is subverted.

Comic books work particularly well because they're already essentially preproduction story boards. Movies are a visual medium just like comic books. Also, if I'm going to plunk down $10/head to see something in the theater, I want some spectacle in my escapism to take advantage of the giant screen and sound system--when I'm in the mood for pre-recorded stage plays, I can do those at home via DVD/streaming.

Also, there're still plenty of cowboy/pioneer movies: The Revenant, True Grit, Django Unchained, Hateful 8, A Million Ways to Die in the West, etc. They're just not the majority of movies because there are so many more movies being made than before. Movies have become a successful medium and they're getting cheaper to produce--witness the growing indie film sub-industry and e.g., the work of various YouTubers. It's not surprising that there are more types of stories being told than in the earlier days since there are more opportunities to tell any given story.

Personally, I almost always prefer the original books and comics to their film adaptations. I'm one of those wierdos who enjoys reading, because I like exercising my imagination when the author describes characters and scenes. From what I can tell, for the average person finds reading to be a chore: bothersome, unenjoyable, tedious. They crave the stories and characters, but have no desire to put forth the time and effort in reading a book.

Thus we have film adaptations that compress days of reading and thought process into two to three hours. Because they never read the source material, they do not notice or care about the stuff that is missing, flat out wrong, or altered to fit snugly into that two hour window.

People enjoy the films largely for the same reasons readers enjoy books: intriguing characters and storylines, dramatic scenes and introspective dialogue. Hollywood loves film adaptations because readers pick these books and comics basically tell everyone that they have everything needed to make an enjoyable experience, so Hollywood knows that even a mediocre adaptation will still likely be a huge income for them.

In short, so long as people are too lazy or too rushed to read a book, and so long as hollywood can continue to profit off the adaptations, they will never go away.

That said, no movie has ever moved me to the verge of tears the way a book can. Movies can make me feel anxiety and apprehension, but they have never made me feel true fear. The climax of Steven Erickson's "Deadhouse Gates" made my throat tight, my eyes tear up, and my heart lurch. Brave New World made me feel fear for a world that was not my own and yet easily could be, and sorrow at the fate of those who do not conform to such a world.

I have never known a movie to surpass the original work.
